questions.a: A push or pull on an object, arising from interaction between two objects.

questions.q: Name two effects a force can produce.
questions.a: It can move or stop an object, and change its speed, direction or shape.

questions.q: Is force a push only, a pull only, or both?
questions.a: Both - pushing a swing and pulling a rope are both forces.

concepts.title: What a Force Can Do to Objects

questions.q: How can a force change the shape of an object?
questions.a: Squeezing or stretching changes shape - pressing dough, stretching a rubber band.

questions.q: Give an example where force changes an object's direction.
questions.a: A batsman's hit turns the ball's direction; so does a steering wheel turning a car.

questions.q: Can a force act without changing motion? When?
questions.a: Yes - balanced forces (equal and opposite) leave the state of motion unchanged.

questions.q: Name two contact forces and two non-contact forces.
questions.a: Contact: muscular force, friction. Non-contact: gravity, magnetism (and electrostatic force).

questions.q: Which force pulls a dropped mango to the ground?
What contact force stops a rolling marble?
questions.a: Friction between the marble and the floor.
The pull of gravity on a body, measured with a spring balance in newtons.

questions.q: How do weight and mass differ?
questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter (kg), fixed everywhere; weight is a force (N) that changes with gravity.

questions.q: Why does a person weigh less on the moon?
questions.a: The moon's gravity is weaker (about one-sixth), so the pull on the body is less.

questions.q: Why do some objects float and others sink?
questions.a: Those less dense than the liquid float; denser ones sink.

questions.q: Why does a heavy ship float but a small nail sink?
questions.a: The ship's shape traps air, making its average density less than water; the nail is denser.
The upward push a fluid gives a body placed in it; it decides floating.
